#1815. Senegal champions again, but Morocco’s phone call allegation could open a new legal fight

By Alexis Pereira | 24 Nov 2026 16:33

Senegal have been officially restored as champions of Africa. The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) delivered its verdict on Tuesday 24 November and sided with the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF), overturning the decision by the Confederation of African Football (CAF) that had awarded the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations to Morocco on a technicality. The Lions keep the title they won on the pitch in Rabat.

It is a dramatic twist in a case that had poisoned African football since January. By cancelling the CAF appeal board’s decision of 17 March 2026, CAS sided with the Senegalese federation. The original result of the final is therefore restored: a 1-0 win for Senegal after extra time.

The Lausanne-based court rejected the regulatory reading that had led CAF to penalise the Lions with a forfeit. It found that Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON regulations, used by CAF’s appeal committee, were not applicable in this case, and that only the restart of play authorised by the final’s referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala, counted.

‘By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume,’ the court said. ‘In the Panel’s view, there is no doubt that the effects of the Referee’s decision were limited to the pitch. As such, the Panel considers that the Referee’s decision was covered by the “field of play” doctrine.’

The doctrine gives priority to decisions made on the pitch unless there is evidence that the rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith. CAS said Articles 82 and 84 were only meant to determine the outcome of a match when a team’s behaviour leads the referee to declare that play has definitively stopped, and so did not apply. ‘In conclusion, the panel considers that in resuming the match, the referee did not err in law,’ the court added.

The panel acknowledged that the referee had to decide in a climate of extreme tension, but said that did not make the decision arbitrary and that his judgement did not appear to have been affected by factors outside the game. On the disciplinary side, it recalled that the FSF, coach Pape Thiaw and some players had already been sanctioned by CAF in separate disciplinary proceedings. The FSF appeal was therefore upheld, and the decision was unanimous.

On 18 January 2026, Senegal beat Morocco in the final thanks to an extra-time goal from Pape Gueye. Before that goal, the match had turned in stoppage time when referee Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty after a VAR intervention. Furious, coach Thiaw told his players to leave the pitch. After an interruption of around 16 minutes, the Senegalese returned, led by Sadio Mane. Brahim Diaz then missed the Moroccan penalty before Gueye decided the final.

The Moroccan federation (FRMF) immediately contested the match. After its first complaint was rejected by the disciplinary committee, CAF’s appeal board declared Morocco the winners and Senegal forfeited on 17 March, applying Articles 82 and 84 of the competition regulations. The FSF went to CAS on 25 March, and a closed-door hearing took place on 8 October.

The ruling restores Senegal’s status as African champions, giving them a second AFCON after their 2022 triumph in Cameroon. The team, now coached by Patrick Vieira, has two continental titles.

For Morocco, the verdict is a heavy blow. The host nation, which hoped to win a second crown 50 years after its first in 1976, sees the pitch result confirmed and remains credited with one title. But the case may not have said its last word.

A few hours before the verdict, the FRMF reported an ‘incident’. According to RMC, the federation denounces an alleged telephone conversation on Sunday between Ulrich Haas, one of the judges appointed to the case, and Abdoulaye Fall, president of the FSF. If proven, that contact could be a flaw Morocco might exploit before the Swiss Federal Tribunal, which can review CAS decisions on procedural grounds.

For its part, CAS says it received no report from Morocco. It remains to be seen whether the controversy marks the start of a new legal saga.

#1813. Four first half goals for Hassocks in hammering of Hurst

Four first half goals away at Billingshurst showed Hassocks have not suffered any lasting damage from their midweek hammering in the Sussex Transport Senior Cup at the hands of Chichester City.

Chi relentlessly stuck six past the Robins on Tuesday night. Hassocks were equally unforgiving on Hurst, pocketing all three points before the half time whistle.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

No further goals were added nor needed after the break, allowing the Robins to take their foot of the pedal and James Westlake to rattle through the substitutions ahead of a huge upcoming five weeks which could be season-defining.

Hassocks go to Rusthall next Saturday for their first ever appearance in the third round of the FA Vase. A place in the last 32 of the national competition is up for grabs.

December then brings matches against Roffey, Guernsey, East Grinstead Town, Eastbourne United and Haywards Heath Town. Five games against teams in the top eight of the Southern Combination Premier Division all harbouring hopes of promotion.

"It's going to be busy, it's going to be hard," said James Westlake of those upcoming fixtures. "It is a tough run through until January time really. But those big games in the league are the ones we want to be competing in."

Billingshurst provided a different type of challenge. Several ingredients were there for a banana skin - a pitch already heavy before kick off, opposition fighting relegation and a popular former Robin in the home dugout.

Eddie French expressed his displeasure at the performance of the officials afterwards and it was hard not to have some sympathy for the ex-Hassocks favourite.

Certainly in relation to the bizarre series of decisions which saw the Robins awarded a penalty for their second goal of the afternoon, Nat Guest sent off and Billingshurst left to play for 70 minutes with 10 men.

Hassocks took the lead five minutes prior to that pivotal sequence of events. Playing down the hill, Omar Abdsami exchanged a one-two with Dan Perry to split open the centre of the Hurst defence.

Abdsami still needed to get around covering right back James Bendell. He did that via some quick feet before firing low and hard across Fraser Trigwell and into the far corner.

Trigwell provided another current link between the clubs whilst Hassocks introduced former Hurst midfielder Luke Brodie from their bench in the second half.

Then came the major talking point. Lewis Finney delivered a corner which Dan Turner met with a towering header. The ball was several feet over the line when it struck Guest in the hand.

Remarkably, the officials did not award the goal but instead gave the Robins a spot kick and sent Guest off for deliberate hand ball.

Chaos ensued with the surreal scenario of both Hassocks and Billingshurst players protesting against the same decision for different reasons.

Once order was restored, Finney put away the spot kick despite Trigwell diving the right way. And just to really rub salt into Hurst wounds, the initial corner Turner scored from was a clear goal kick too.

"I would certainly have been frustrated if that went against us with the awarding of the corner to start it all off," Westlake said afterwards.

"If you are a neutral watching the game, you would ask that the goal from Turner is given and it is not a sending off. It was a shame for them but I guess we already had a good foothold and would have been 2-0 up anyway."

Two very quickly became three and there was nothing controversial about the spectacular strike from Finney 120 seconds after his successful penalty.

Liam Hendy played a long ball forward which Perry won in the air. The flick dropped into the path of Finney, who hit a 25 yard dipping volley. Trigwell got a hand to it but could not keep it out.

Hassocks enjoyed near-total domination for the remainder of the first half with the Billingshurst X account posting at the interval: "To say this has been like the Alamo would be harsh on the Alamo as it has been more one-sided than that."

Tall striker Jamie Wilkes lent so far back that he was almost horizontal when putting a shot from a good position into orbit. Trigwell then made an excellent finger tip save diving low at his near post to keep out an Abdsami effort.

Having set up both Abdsami and Finney, Perry added the fourth himself five minutes before half time. Jack Troak started the move down the left and his square pass inside was beautifully back heeled to Finney by Darren Budd.

Finney glided past Jack Griffin and although Trigwell did well to parry away the shot, Perry followed up for a poacher's finish to open his Hassocks account.

Billingshurst will undoubtedly be happy to see the back of the Hitman. Five weeks ago he scored a hat-trick against them for East Grinstead Town with what turned out to be his final goals in a Wasps shirt.

French changed Hurst's shape for the second half and it allowed them to stem the flow of goals without ever really offering much going forward.

Ed Cooper did not have a serious save to make although Griffin and Kieran Britland both should have done better when shooting high and wide respectively.

Britland did at least have the excuse of losing his footing as he pulled the trigger. He was not the only one to slip and slide as the already challenging surface cut up massively the longer the game went on.

Chances at the other end for Hassocks came for Charlie Bonwick-Adams, who put a header straight at Trigwell. Finney guided a Troak cross wide of the front post and substitute Raging Joe Bull did everything right after overlapping Abdsami, receiving a pass and cutting inside only to shoot into an adjacent field.

Trigwell made an outstanding double save when pushing away a Budd piledriver from the edge of the box at full stretch before reacting quick enough to get up and deflect the follow up from Abdsami behind using his feet.

Turner hit a volley diverted behind by a fine block with the final opportunity of the game involving two more replacements. Lewis Croal headed down a cross for Big Alex Fair to shoot directly upwards rather than towards goal.

"We wanted to kick on in the second half but that obviously wasn't meant to be," Westlake added. "The lads have come off disappointed considering we couldn't score more goals. But a clean sheet, four goals and three points are the really important thing today."

Hassocks: Ed Cooper; Charlie Bonwick-Adams, Dan Turner, Liam Hendy, Jack Troak; Jamie Wilkes, Darren Budd; Devon Fender, Lewis Finney, Omar Abdsami, Dan Perry.

Subs: Liam Benson, Lewis Croal, Joe Bull, Luke Brodie, Alex Fair (used).

Starman: Lewis Finney converted a penalty for the second goal, scored a stunning volley for the third and set up Dan Perry for the fourth.

#1811. Tottenham beat Chelsea again as Lamine Yamal-like wonderkid signs new long-term contract

By Ben Knapton | 24 Nov 2026 16:34

Tottenham Hotspur have confirmed that teenage wonderkid Luca Williams-Barnett has put pen to paper on a new long-term contract with the club.

The 18-year-old extends his terms just three days after a dream full Premier League debut against Ipswich Town, scoring one and setting up another in a 2-0 Tottenham victory.

Against the Tractor Boys, Williams-Barnett became the third-youngest Premier League goalscorer in Tottenham's history, and the second-youngest to score and provide an assist in a PL game for any club after Michael Owen.

Following reports that Williams-Barnett was on the verge of committing his future to the Lilywhites, Tottenham announced on Tuesday that the 2008-born talent had signed his renewal.

Explaining his decision to pen fresh terms, Williams-Barnett said: "This is a special moment for me and my family, and one I have worked really hard to reach. But this is only the start.

Scoring on his first start ? What a moment for Luca Williams-Barnett! https://t.co/m6iALigFuy

"Spurs is a family to me. I've been here for so long – it's a second home, where I trust the people and coaches who have pushed me to become the player I am today. The Club has trusted and believed in me, now I'm ready to repay that."

Head coach Roberto De Zerbi - who previously compared Williams-Barnett to Lamine Yamal - added: “Luca is a player I think the world of, and I'm so happy that he has signed a new contract.

“He has benefitted from being around the first team every day, growing in stature and consistency, and has deserved his place in the matchday squad over recent weeks.

“Everyone can see how technically gifted Luca is on the pitch but I also love his calmness and decision-making under pressure.

“The best players have confidence on the pitch and humility off it. There is still plenty of room for Luca to improve, and I know he will continue to work hard every day to be the best version of himself."

Williams-Barnett joined the Tottenham academy setup from Luton Town in 2018 and made his debut for the senior side in a 3-0 EFL Cup third-round win over Doncaster Rovers in September 2025.

The teenager has since played five times for the Tottenham first team and has won six caps for England's Under-19s, scoring two goals and providing one assist at that level.

Williams-Barnett's previous Tottenham deal was due to expire in 2028, although it is not clear how many years the teenager's extension is worth.

Nevertheless, Tottenham have fended off interest from Chelsea and Borussia Dortmund to keep hold of their academy graduate, and talks over fresh terms began before De Zerbi integrated him into his first-team squad.

Williams-Barnett is expected to keep his place in Tottenham's starting lineup in Sunday's clash against Sunderland, for which De Zerbi may be facing a new James Maddison concern.

#1809. Raith Rovers charged by Scottish FA over crude post aimed at Neil Lennon

Raith Rovers have been charged by the Scottish Football Association over a social media post mocking Dunfermline Athletic manager Neil Lennon in the aftermath of the Fife derby.

Following the 0-0 draw at Stark's Park on November 6, Lennon made a pinching gesture with his thumb and forefinger towards rival supporters which was widely interpreted as a jibe calling Raith Rovers a "small club".

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Shortly after the final whistle, Raith's official X account shared a photo of Lennon making the gesture alongside the caption, "How big is your penis, Neil?". The club deleted the post 52 minutes later after it went viral.

The SFA compliance officer has now issued the Kirkcaldy outfit with a notice of complaint relating to a breach of Disciplinary Rule 73, which reads: "No recognised football body, club, official, Team Official or other member of Team Staff, player, match official or other person under the jurisdiction of the Scottish FA shall in an interview, a ‘blog’ on the internet, on a social networking or micro-blogging site, or in any other manner calculated or likely to lead to publicity, make comment(s) of a discriminatory or offensive nature based on, but not limited to, race, ethnicity, religion, gender, sexual orientation or disability, or that endorse or encourage foul play or violent Conduct or are otherwise offensive.

"There shall be a presumption that any material published in such a manner was published in the name of and/or with the authority of the person or body bearing to have published the material."

Sanctions typically start at a £500 lower-end fine and rise up to a £5,000 top-end fine.

Speaking about the incident last week, Lennon described the episode as "embarrassing for them", referring to Raith, adding; "“You know, that’s like an official club Twitter account, which is embarrassing. I’ll say no more than that.”

Raith are scheduled to face a Hampden disciplinary hearing on December 17. This falls just over a week before the two sides meet again at East End Park on Boxing Day.

#1808. Charalampos Kostoulas identifies Brighton turning point under Fabian Hurzeler after James Milner trust

Brighton striker Charalampos Kostoulas believes earning the trust of his teammates has been just as important as his goals this season.

The 19-year-old has made an encouraging start to the 2026-27 campaign, with five goals and three assists in 14 appearances across all competitions as he establishes himself as an increasingly important figure in Fabian Hurzeler's side.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

It marks a significant step forward from his first season at the Amex Stadium, when he scored twice in 21 Premier League appearances, making just two starts.

Brighton head coach Hurzeler - who last season questioned Kostoulas’ commitment to training - is now impressed by the progress, particularly the forward's growing physical strength, work rate and understanding of the demands of English football.

But Kostoulas says there has been no dramatic change to his game. Instead, he has gradually learned what the team requires from him and become more comfortable in his role.

"Mainly, it's about understanding what the team wants," he said to Sussex World.

"For me, as a striker, with time and after some months, I started to understand that. With the minutes I've got and things like that, I gained the trust of my teammates and I want to keep going like that."

Hurzeler has previously highlighted the difference in the youngster's ability to compete physically, saying: "When you see him now and how resilient he is in personal duels, it's something completely different."

The Brighton boss has also praised his pressing and attitude towards improvement, describing a player who is becoming increasingly professional.

Kostoulas credits the manager's clarity and attention to detail, while revealing he has enjoyed the greater freedom given to him in the attacking role.

"He's clear with the instructions he gives on the pitch. He's always clear," he said.

"But I think I didn't change the way I was playing. Last season I could also do these types of things on the pitch, but I have more of a free role, especially in my position. I like it."

The transition from Olympiacos to Brighton was not without its challenges, however.

Kostoulas admits the biggest adjustment was the daily routine, with longer hours at the training ground, different training methods and a greater emphasis on meetings and preparation.

"The daily routine, I think, was the hardest," he told Sussex World. "We spend many hours at the training ground, more than I was used to in Greece.

"There are different types of training, a different approach to the game, more meetings and things like that."

He was helped by some of Brighton's more experienced players, with former midfielder James Milner playing a particularly important role during his first season.

"Most of the older players would come and say something to me as advice," Kostoulas explained. "Last season, James Milner was speaking a lot to me and trying to help me."

He still occasionally speaks to Milner, while Pascal Gross has also become an important figure in his development.

For Kostoulas, having someone to turn to is vital when moving to a different country and footballing culture.

"It's important to have someone to help you understand the way the team works here," he explained to Sussex World.

"It's totally different. If someone from here moves to Greece, they will also need time. It will be hard for them.

"You have to find someone you can trust, have a good relationship with, speak to and who can give you an understanding of most of the things here and what's expected."

There is also the prospect of sharing the pitch with fellow Greek forward Stefanos Tsitsimas, whose return from a lengthy spell out has delighted Kostoulas.

"I'm really happy for him," he said. "He has a really good mindset and I have big trust in him. I think he will do great."

Kostoulas was keen to avoid looking too far ahead when asked about Brighton's ambitions after their impressive start to the season.

Rather than focus on the possibility of challenging at the top of the table or making a deep run in Europe, he insists the squad are concentrating on the next match.

"We don't think about what will happen after six months when the season will be finished," he said to Sussex World.

"We're just enjoying every day, trying to be happy and win as many games as we can."

#1806. Besiktas vs Hapoel Be'er Sheva - prediction, team news, lineups

By Joshua Cole | 24 Nov 2026 16:46, Last updated: 24 Nov 2026 16:46

Besiktas will be looking to strengthen their position in the UEFA Europa League's top eight when they face Hapoel Be'er Sheva at Batumi Stadium on Thursday evening.

The Turkish giants sit eighth in the league-phase standings with seven points from four matches, while Beer-Sheva are 33rd with just one point and will be desperate to keep their slim hopes of reaching the knockout stages alive.

Besiktas have made a reasonably encouraging start to their Europa League campaign, winning two of their opening four matches, although their recent results have been somewhat inconsistent across competitions.

The Turkish side began their league-phase campaign with an emphatic 4-1 victory over Marseille before producing another impressive performance to beat Hoffenheim 3-2 away from home.

However, they were unable to maintain that momentum when they hosted Crystal Palace, settling for a 2-2 draw despite having opportunities to secure all three points, while their most recent European outing proved equally frustrating as they suffered a 3-2 defeat away to Celtic.

Besiktas have subsequently responded positively in domestic competition, recording a 3-0 home victory over Genclerbirligi before producing an impressive attacking display to beat Konyaspor 4-2 away from home last time out.

Vincenzo Italiano's side will be confident of securing another positive result against Beer-Sheva, particularly given the Israeli side's struggles in the competition and the hosts' perfect head-to-head record in this fixture.

The previous meetings between these sides took place in the 2016-17 Europa League round of 32, when Besiktas secured a 3-1 away victory before recording a 2-1 triumph in the return fixture to complete a 5-2 aggregate success.

The fixture is set to be played at Batumi Stadium in Georgia rather than Besiktas's usual home ground in Istanbul, with the venue change implemented for security reasons following consultations between UEFA and the Turkish authorities.

Beer-Sheva, meanwhile, have endured a difficult European campaign, collecting just one point from their opening four matches and remaining outside the knockout playoff positions.

Ran Kozuch's side began their league-phase campaign with a goalless draw against Dinamo Zagreb, but they have subsequently suffered three consecutive defeats in the competition.

Their first setback came against AZ Alkmaar, when they lost 2-1 on the road, before enduring a disappointing 4-0 defeat against Union Saint-Gilloise, and they were unable to respond against OFI Crete, suffering a 2-0 home defeat.

Beer-Sheva have also struggled to produce consistent performances domestically, losing 1-0 against Hapoel Tel Aviv after previously recording impressive victories over Maccabi Petah Tikva and Maccabi Haifa.

The visitors will need to improve considerably in the final third if they are to trouble Besiktas, particularly after failing to score in their last two Europa League matches.

Beer-Sheva have also struggled away from home in the Europa League main draw, losing nine of their last 11 matches on their travels while drawing the other two.

Hapoel Be'er Sheva form (all competitions):

Besiktas will be without Umit Akdag, who is suspended for Thursday's encounter, while every other player is available for the Black Eagles.

Junior Olaitan has scored or assisted in all four of his Europa League main-draw appearances for the hosts and could become just the second African player since 2009-10 to achieve that feat in his first five such matches in the competition.

Dusan Vlahovic will hope to continue his rich scoring form after netting a brace against Konyaspor, taking his tally to four goals in his last two matches.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva will be without Eliel Peretz, who has been sidelined since late October with a groin injury, while Dan Biton remains unavailable due to a heart-related problem.

Matan Baltaxa is also a doubt after sustaining a foot injury, while Ofir Marciano is expected to remain sidelined with a calf problem.

Nubel; Murillo, Bulut, Topcu, R Yilmaz; Ndidi; Trossard, Kocku, Olaitan, Fakili; Vlahovic

Hapoel Be'er Sheva possible starting lineup:

Marciano; Mizrahi, Vitor, Nachmias, Amador; Amankwah, Yehoshua, Ahmed; East, Zlatanovic, Ganah

Besiktas possess greater attacking quality and head into this encounter on the back of consecutive domestic victories, while Beer-Sheva's struggles in Europe and their poor away record suggest that the visitors could have a difficult evening in Georgia, with Italiano's side expected to secure a comfortable victory.

#1805. Eastbourne Borough warm hearts on cold night – as professional job sees off Aveley

Sometimes the arithmetic scarcely adds up. Saturday afternoon in the sunshine: for sharing eight goals in a lavish celebration of the sport, one point. Tuesday night in temperatures that froze the breath and numbed the fingers: for a routine 3-1 victory: three points.

But Borough's players, management and frozen supporters were not complaining. Steve King's side had played positively, stood up strong against physically powerful opponents, and they got all the unglamorous things right.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

A smart move for 1-0 on 24 minutes, and after an Aveley equaliser, a second goal on the stroke of half-time. And a superb Kai Corbett strike early in the second half to put clear distance between the teams.

Aveley were always chasing the game - and chase it they did - but the Sports deserved their victory, and King's squad now sit third in the division, three points behind leaders Welling but with a game in hand.

Credit, too, to the 529 hardy souls who wrapped themselves in layers of scarves, coats and headgear to enjoy a proper football contest in which the visitors also played their part. Team sport is for sharing - and just a little bit of shared suffering to cheer on your team.

King chose to shuffle the pack a little on for Aveley's visit. Liam Nash, Max Sheaf and Darren McQueen took a rest, and the manager bolstered his midfield with the return of Craig Eastmond. Paul McCallum took a lone striker role - although with ample support from the players around him. Aveley, robust and physically strong, lined up with a proper old-fashioned 4-4-2.

Early stages were quite cagey, but a goalmouth melee on 12 minutes saw Corbett's low effort cleared, and the momentum was with Borough.

Corbett, two-goal hero on Saturday, found Aveley doubling up on him: The Millers' staff had done their homework. And with the industrious visitors defending from the front, as the coaching jargon calls it, the Sports needed to turn possession into scoring chances.

But the patience and persistence finally brought reward on 24 minutes. Corbett's corner was met first by Elliott Johnson and then McCallum, but with Aveley throwing bodies on the line, both were blocked. But the second block fell invitingly for Freddie Carter, who blasted his shot high into the roof of the net.

Aveley had spent much of the first half-hour bravely covering, blocking, spoiling – but the 15 minutes before half-time saw the Essex side pushing forward and suddenly threatening to open up the Sports defence. On 40 minutes they swept through the inside-right channel and a lovely cross from Anthony Jeffery was met by big striker Matt Johnson for 1-1.

Borough's response was almost immediate: with the Priory Lane scoreboard glowing on 45 minutes, a sweet move into the final third was prompted by Matt Hayden, Eastbourne's gleeful young full-back, who found Terrell Egbri on the right. The bustling winger delivered a lovely cross, met by skipper Josh Rees with an unstoppable diving header to restore the lead.

The second half resumed as the first had left off - or almost. Aveley are a resilient, physical outfit - within the laws and spirit of the game - and they came at Borough with renewed impetus.

Question: would a single goal lead see the Sports survive a whole 45 minutes? Answer: Corbett. From a set-piece, the hero of Enfield slalomed through a ridiculously tight penalty area to deliver a rocket into the top left corner of the Mllers' net.

Aveley did have their chances - or at least the promising approach work. But they could not quite find that final piercing pass to open up the home defence, and Borough were disciplined, alert and resilient.

A night to freeze the breath. A match to warm Borough hearts. And with 22 victories in 24 games, King's men have the momentum, the belief, and that mental force-field to carry them into the deepest of Decembers and out the other side.

#1804. Rangers half-time surgery sparks second half tempest to subdue Ibrox anxiety

There are evenings when tactical blueprints dissolve into sheer, unscripted theatre, and for 45 minutes at a rain-soaked Ibrox, it appeared as though Derek McInnes’ best-laid plans had conspired against his own side. Yet by the time a frenetic second half had run its course, Rangers had conjured an epic turnaround to claim a breathless 3–2 victory over Aberdeen that saw them move within a point of idle Premiership leaders Celtic.

In testing conditions, both sides abandoned any pretence of caution to serve up a thrilling second half that was in stark contrast to the opening 45 minutes, which offered little beyond frustration and creeping anxiety for the Rangers manager.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Facing the club where he spent eight formative years in the dugout, McInnes had tinkered with his starting formation, handing Ben Godfrey a first start since July 31st as part of a three-man defence designed to counter their opponents narrow, winger-less system, However, the hosts looked entirely disjointed.

Rangers, playing their first home match in a full month following an unusual sequence of five consecutive away fixtures, began on the front foot. However, despite Dan Neil squandering a glorious opportunity from six yards inside the opening 60 seconds, his rebound subsequently struck off teammate Ryan Naderi, the home side struggled to establish rhythm or coherence.

Aberdeen, aiming to build on their first win under new head coach Mario Frick at the weekend, sensed vulnerability and grew steadily in conviction. Organised in a compact 4-3-1-2 shape, the visitors frustrated Rangers before delivering a clinical blow on the half-hour mark. Brad Lyons capitalised on Rangers’ hesitation from a corner to produce a diving header that was hooked off the line by Nico Raskin. However, after VAR intervened, the ball was adjudged to have crossed the line and referee John Beaton awarded the goal, sparking wild celebrations scenes in the away end.

Worse almost followed for the hosts. Only profligacy in front of goal, most notably from Moroccan striker Ayoub Mouloua, who twice spurned clear openings before the interval, prevented the Dons from carrying a more commanding lead into the break as the Rangers supporters made their dissatisfaction known.

If the first half belonged to Aberdeen’s disciplined industry, the opening 12 minutes of the second belonged to Rangers’ ruthless efficiency. McInnes wasted little time in rectifying his questionable team selection, executing a bold triple substitution at half-time that saw Kim Min-su, Tuur Rommens and Findlay Curtis replace Kevin Kelsy, Godfrey, and Badredine Bouanani.

The transformation was instantaneous. Within 60 seconds of the restart, Min-su tested Aberdeen goalkeeper Marius Müller with a dipping shot. Müller could only parry the ball directly into the path of Ryan Naderi, who gleefully dispatched the rebound from close range to restore parity.

Before Aberdeen could draw breath, Ibrox erupted once more. Just 64 seconds after the equaliser, Naderi turned provider, threading an incisive pass into Djeidi Gassama. Outpacing his man, the winger kept his composure to drill a low finish across Müller into the far corner. In barely a minute, a packed stadium that had been growing increasingly restless was suddenly alive again.

Rangers’ third arrived in the 56th minute via a devastating counter-attack. Min-su, whose introduction had injected vital urgency into the hosts' attacking play, won possession deep inside his own half and drove up field before releasing Gassama. Cutting the ball neatly across the penalty area, the Mauritanian international teed up Raskin, who coolly side-footed low across Müller to establish a seemingly decisive 3-1 advantage.

Aberdeen, however, refused to crumble. Barely a minute after Raskin’s goal, Alexander Briedl drifted inside from the left flank and slipped a weighted pass into the path of Findlay Marshall. The youngster met it cleanly, sending a crisp drive crashing in off the post to reduce the deficit and reignite a pulsating contest.

What followed was a nerve-shredding final half-hour punctuated by transitions and agonising near-misses. Aberdeen’s Nesta Guinness-Walker endured frustration when his late penalty appeal was waved away. In between, Marshall came within inches of securing a share of the spoils, dragging a left-footed effort agonisingly wide of Pandur's post in the closing stages after the Croatian had made a spectacular save to deny Nicky Devlin from a corner at his front post.

If Scottish football occasionally stands accused of predictability, nobody among the 50,738 crowd could reasonably complain of short measure. Rangers survived, although not without making their supporters endure another uncomfortable finale as they took advantage of their game in hand to move closer to keeper their title challenge firmly on track.

Dundee – hurting from Saturday’s 8-0 hammering by Hearts – put up a fight after the interval and Joe Wright’s strike gave them hope of a comeback.

“We wanted to give ourselves a foundation to build from and we gave ourselves that.

“We were much more cohesive in the second half and when you suffer the defeat we suffered on Saturday and you come here and you find yourself 2-0 down at half-time, it asks a lot of questions of you as a group and I thought they responded brilliantly.

#1801. Ajax vs Thun - prediction, team news, lineups

By Adepoju Marvellous | 24 Nov 2026 16:54, Last updated: 25 Nov 2026 17:25

Ajax and Thun face off at the Johan Cruyff Arena on Thursday as the 2026-27 Conference League campaign reaches its midway point.

Both teams emerged victorious in their last continental outings and now look to build on that momentum on the European stage.

Returning to action after agonisingly surrendering a two-goal lead to FC Twente before the international break, Ajax made light work of Eredivisie newcomers ADO Den Haag, cruising to a 3-0 victory on Sunday thanks to two goals from Davy Klaassen and a strike from Jorthy Mokio.

Michel’s side have now claimed six victories from their last seven matches in all competitions since losing to Hajduk Split in their Conference League opener in mid-October, with subsequent continental outings yielding wins over Atalanta and Midtjylland by a combined score of 8-1.

Central to De Godenzonen’s resurgence has been their ability to start quickly, with Klaassen's opener last time out marking the seventh consecutive match in which they have broken the deadlock.

Ajax currently sit outside the guaranteed knockout places in the Conference League and will be keen to collect maximum points to break into the top eight, thereby avoiding the additional hurdle of a playoff tie in an already congested campaign.

Thursday’s game marks the third meeting between the sides, with the hosts seeking to maintain their perfect record in this fixture, having come out on top in both group-stage encounters of the 2005-06 Champions League en route to a last-16 exit.

Thun ended a 13-year absence from European competition by qualifying for this season’s Conference League, but a pair of 1-0 defeats in their opening two matches against FC Twente and Hajduk Split meant their return to continental action began on a sour note.

Days after scoring four times in the final 20 minutes of a nine-goal thriller against Lausanne-Sport to claim a remarkable triumph, Gian-Luca Privitelli's men claimed a 3-1 victory against Scottish outfit Hearts to finally get their European campaign up and running at the third attempt.

Back-to-back winless games against Basel and Young Boys have followed, so Die Oberlander head to Amsterdam with confidence low and knowing that a defeat could see them drop out of the knockout playoff places, so there is little margin for error.

Thun have conceded in each of their last 13 competitive matches, including 11 goals in their most recent four. Tightening up defensively will be essential if the Swiss side are to end their ongoing three-game losing run against Dutch opponents.

Thursday’s visitors have let in just one goal after half time across their three Conference League games so far, but against an Ajax side who have netted seven times in that period, they cannot afford any lapses in concentration over the course of the 90 minutes.

Attacking trio Simon Adingra, Kasper Dolberg, and Viktor Tsygankov are all ruled out through injury for Ajax, who welcomed back Anton Gaaei and Julian Brandt last time out.

Having only joined in mid-September, Yves Bissouma was not registered by the hosts for European competition, making him ineligible to feature on Thursday.

Tolu Arokodare has a tournament-high five direct goal contributions in the Conference League this term, and despite failing to find the net against ADO, he remains one to watch.

Genis Montolio and Fabio Saiz remain unavailable for Thun as they continue to recover from long-term knee injuries.

Furkan Dursun (leg) and Mattias Kait (back) both missed the visitors’ defeat to Young Boys, and neither is expected to return for Thursday.

Ter Stegen; Rosa, Kehrer, Janse, Wijndal; Klaassen, Baas; Gloukh, Mokio, Ouazane; Arokodare

Ajax are in imperious form and have won each of their last three home matches without conceding.

While the hosts may concede this time around, we fully expect them to claim victory and keep their momentum going.

#1798. Derek McInnes airs his Rangers frustrations and ‘biggest takeaway’ as new Aberdeen boss makes ‘beatable’ claim

Derek McInnes has warned his Rangers side they must learn to control games more efficiently for longer periods if they are to sustain their Scottish Premiership title challenge this season.

The Ibrox manager praised the resilience of his players after they managed to overturn a half-time deficit to beat a revitalised Aberdeen 3-2 in a thrilling contest, courtesy of a decisive ten-minute goal blitz early in the second half.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

However, McInnes was frustrated that Rangers allowed their opponents back quickly into the contest after establishing a seemingly unassailable cushion, which left them clinging on during an increasingly anxious finale.

Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin turned the game around, before Findlay Marshall's immediate response ensured the Dons went down fighting.

Despite the satisfaction of extending their unbeaten run to 14 matches, McInnes was unhappy with the manner in which his team surrendered control, insisting his players put unnecessary pressure on themselves.

“Delighted we've got the job done. Great win for us in the end,” he said. “Disappointed we've allowed ourselves to be hanging on at the end rather than controlling the game. The question was being asked of us at half-time. We were in a difficult spot. We were having to dig it deep and you find out about your players in these sort of situations. It's good to know that we have dug that result out.

“We need to recognise that we need to be better for longer periods, particularly at Ibrox. By conceding the second goal, we should still stay on the job, but with too many negative passes, too many backwards passes, we need to own that a wee bit.

"The biggest takeaway for me tonight is my players had to dig deep. We were in a tough spot at half-time, 50,000, 1-0 down at home to Aberdeen. That's not an easy place to be. It's alright for me to try and address it tactically, having a go at half-time or whatever, but they've still got to go and deliver, and they delivered a big performance.”

McInnes had initially opted for a system designed to exploit the spaces around Aberdeen's front two, with Gassama and Badredine Bouanani providing width on both flanks. However, he conceded that his side had not been productive enough despite repeatedly getting into promising positions in the final third before a triple half-time substitution altered the formation to provide greater control in central areas.

“I thought the subs helped us and I thought for 20 minutes we were outstanding,” McInnes added. “We showed the speed, the intensity, the quality, the intelligence. We blew them away.”

New Aberdeen head coach Mario Frick was left frustrated by his side’s collapse immediately after half-time, but felt they had shown enough to suggest Rangers were there for the taking.

“I am disappointed with the five or six minutes after half-time. That hurts,” he stated. “We saw a good performance, Rangers were beatable tonight. We need more time. We have to improve. We have to talk about those ten minutes.

“After 3-1 down we came back and we believed in ourselves. We deserved the equaliser. We came to win and we are disappointed to go back with zero points. I see a lot of positives things.”

#1796. I watched Rangers edge five-goal thriller vs Aberdeen and noted a title-winning trait and blossoming talent

Rangers produced a quickfire second-half comeback to beat Aberdeen 3-2 at Ibrox and move to within a point of Scottish Premiership leaders Celtic on Tuesday night.

After trailing to Brad Lyons' first-half header, which was deemed to have crossed the line by VAR despite Nico Raskin’s attempt to clear the ball, the hosts struck three times in a blistering spell after the interval through Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Raskin.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Findlay Marshall's immediate reply ensured a tense finale, but Rangers held on to secure a vital three points and extend their unbeaten run to 14 matches. Derek McInnes’ side now have the chance to move top of the table on Saturday when they host high-flying Falkirk.

Lewis Anderson watched the action unfold for The Scotsman and picks out his three main takeaways from an absorbing five-goal thriller.

Once again, Rangers found a way to win. Their impressive run of results in recent months has been built on an increasingly familiar trait: an ability to secure three points even when performances fall short of the required standard. Against an enterprising Aberdeen outfit, however, McInnes' men were given a proper examination before eventually claiming another victory.

McInnes' decision to started with a back three, with Ben Godfrey drafted into the starting line-up for the first time since late July, raised eyebrows and ultimately failed to provide the defensive solidity he would have hoped for. The Dons repeatedly found opportunities to exploit the space around Rangers' exposed backline, particularly during a first half in which the visitors looked the more purposeful side.

Aberdeen played with an intensity that unsettled the hosts. Rangers’ combinations lacked precision, their wide players failed to make a sufficient impact and their build-up play was too laboured to trouble their opponents consistently.

McInnes’ response was decisive, with Kim Min-Su, Findlay Curtis and Tuur Rommens introduced at half-time. It signalled an acknowledgement that significant changes were required. Rangers emerged with greater urgency and attacking intent, and Naderi's equaliser provided the spark for a thrilling turnaround.

For a spell, Rangers looked capable of putting the contest beyond doubt, taking full advantage of the momentum generated by their early second-half goals. Yet just as they appeared to have wrestled the match under control, another defensive lapse allowed Aberdeen to threaten a comeback.

The victory was never entirely comfortable, nor was the performance perfect. But Rangers' capacity to respond to adversity and find a way remains an increasingly valuable asset. They continue to collect the points needed to maintain their title challenge and now have the opportunity to move to the top of the Premiership before Celtic take to the pitch this weekend.

Aberdeen will return north frustrated by the outcome, but newly-appointed head coach Mario Frick can take considerable encouragement from a performance which offered a glimpse of what his side might become under his stewardship.

For long periods, the visitors carried a genuine threat on the counter-attack and had sufficient opportunities to leave Ibrox with something to show for their efforts. Their defensive collapse during Rangers' devastating burst after half-time proved costly, with goalkeeper Marius Muller's handling error providing the catalyst for the hosts' revival.

Yet Aberdeen's response was equally striking. Having been left shell-shocked, they gathered themselves and went after Rangers with renewed conviction, refusing to accept that the contest had slipped beyond them. Findlay Marshall's goal, an impressive contribution from a player still only 20, gave them fresh belief and brought the prospect of an unlikely recovery tantalisingly close.

There was a vibrancy about this Aberdeen display which has been conspicuously absent for much of their recent past under Stephen Robinson. They played with ambition, conviction and a willingness to commit bodies forward, while their response to adversity suggested a resilience which Frick will be keen to nurture.

Aside from the damaging 12-minute spell in which Rangers scored three times, the visitors showed plenty of grounds for optimism. Their organisation was better, their pressing purposeful and their attacking play carried a level of intent which repeatedly troubled the hosts’ rear-guard.

The result will sting, not least because they had done enough in spells to believe a point was within their grasp. But there was little about this performance to suggest Frick intends to oversee a cautious rebuilding exercise. If anything, Aberdeen look set to embrace a more adventurous identity, which should please supporters.

Aberdeen have a seriously talented prospect on their hands in 20-year-old Findlay Marshall, who was influential throughout. The midfielder won the corner which led to Lyons' opener before scoring a sublime second-half goal after being picked out by Alexander Briedl, which set up a tense finale.

His energy and attacking intent made him one of Aberdeen's most dangerous players and offered Frick further evidence of the his undoubted potential. Marshall displayed a maturity and composure which belied his age, combining an impressive work rate with an eye for goal. In defeat, he emerged with considerable credit.

The Rangers No.1’s contribution was arguably as important as the three goals at the opposite end. His first-half fingertip save from Ayoub Mouloua prevented Aberdeen establishing a two-goal advantage. The Croatian’s work was not finished there. After the interval, he made a fine stop at his near post to thwart Nicky Devlin before denying Marshall as Aberdeen searched for an equaliser.

Rangers' second-half attacking burst will dominate the headlines, but without Pandur's crucial interventions the outcome could have been very different.

#1795. Arsenal's complacency and a lack of ambition allowed Newcastle a way back and the Gunners were fortunate to escape with a point after paying the price for not killing the game, writes CRAIG HOPE

Published: 15:17 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 16:15 EST, 21 November 2026

Do not invite the hostility, Arsenal were warned. Do not prod the bear. Do not start Bruno Guimaraes. The champions, with a belligerence of their own, ignored all of that and put the grizzly to sleep in a typically smothering first half. Their mistake was in thinking it was dead.

And so, awakened by a half-time rocket from head coach Matthias Jaissle - including three, inspirational changes - Newcastle somehow led by the 62nd minute.

By this point, the two teams were unrecognisable from those who had played out a one-sided opening period, after which Arsenal were 1-0 in front. Mikel Arteta would not have settled for a draw then.

‘We were exceptional in the first half,’ he later said. ‘We have won matches playing much worse than we did here. The intensity, the aggression – we should have been 3-0 or 4-0 up. But right from the start of the second half, we weren’t at the races. We lost duels, gave the ball away and gave them belief.’

Arteta had Noni Madueke to thank for rescuing the point. The winger was his best player throughout and, had he earlier shown the same incision that produced his 78th-minute equaliser, Arsenal would have won. They would have won by half-time, in fact.

So dominant were they, maybe it was complacency. Or maybe there is a lesson here in showing more bloodthirst when on top.

Arteta, you feel, gets more of a kick from suffocating opponents. But during a pulsating second half in which St James’ Park throbbed to the beat of their brilliant team, the hosts grabbed the pillowcase.

Noni Madueke saved Arsenal's blushes with an equaliser against Newcastle in a tough second half on Saturday

‘The second half was pure belief, pure conviction, pure trust in the team-mate,’ said Jaissle, under increased scrutiny amid the presence of chairman Yasir Al-Rumayyan.

‘There were so many ball-wins with a vertical approach and causing them problems. This is the Newcastle DNA.’

Former Newcastle captain Guimaraes - booed after each of his 36, ineffectual touches - was hooked in the 70th minute, and Arsenal were better for their own changes.

The league leaders can absorb this result, of course. Of greater concern for Arteta is an injury to David Raya that requires an MRI scan.

The goalkeeper left the pitch at the same time as Guimaraes, not because of performance, but clutching his shoulder, the upshot of a robust challenge from William Osula. That home forcefulness typified their second half, if not their first.

The Magpies were poor in the first period but a half-time team talk and changes from Matthias Jaissle worked wonders

Bruno Guimaraes earned a hostile reception as he returned to face the side he once captained

There is now concern for the Gunners, with goalkeeper David Raya going off injured

If Newcastle were to beat Arsenal, so suggested the crumbs of pre-match optimism, they would have to start fast.

At least, that was the blueprint of old on red-hot nights such as this. Newcastle started slow. Arsenal weren’t much quicker, but they didn’t have to be. They moved through the gears as the half unfolded and, with it, they began to move through Newcastle.

Arteta likes this sort of game, when it feels like minimum expenditure for maximum return. In short, it was easy. A training-ground drill. Attack versus defence.

Come half-time, Newcastle had not touched the ball in Arsenal’s penalty area. They simply weren’t allowed to.

Saying that, even with permission they would have found a way to pass it straight out of play or shank a cross into the Leazes End.

Newcastle’s first half really was that short on inspiration. There wasn’t too much perspiration, either. And so the home fans booed on the whistle, for a fifth half on the spin at St James’.

NEWCASTLE (4-3-3): Hornicek 5; Dedic 5 (Livramento 46, 7), Thiaw 7, Burn 7, Hall 6 (Botman 90); Miley 7, Steur 6 (Ramsey 46, 7); Murphy 5 (Elanga 46, 6), Willock 7 (Wissa 83), Barnes 7; Osula 6

ARSENAL (4-2-3-1): Raya 5 (Arrizabalaga 70, 5); Timber 6, Konsa 6, Gabriel 6, Calafiori 6; Guimaraes 5 (Lewis-Skelly 70, 7), Rice 6; Madueke 8, Odegaard 7 (Merino 90), Eze 6 (Tzolis 70, 6); Havertz 7 (Gyokeres 90)

Arsenal led by one, and for them that should have been a source of regret.

The goal came when Lewis Hall, despite screams from team-mate Dan Burn to ‘head it, head it’, decided to control, clumsily, on his chest, allowing Kai Havertz to steal. He freed Eberechi Eze and the first-time finish was routine.

The punishment of Hall’s error, however, was ruthless. Six days after bettering Lamine Yamal, England left back Hall was struggling to contain Madueke. In fact, he and each of his comrades could not get close to any of those in red.

So, it was as if two sides had swapped shirts after the break. From nowhere, Newcastle attacked. That may sound basic, but this was seismic. The exclusion zone that had been Arsenal’s penalty box was no longer off limits.

Suddenly, they were able to run, tackle and, yes, shoot. From passive to aggressive, they drew level just four minutes after the restart.

Joe Willock hurried Odegaard into a mistake, William Osula pounced on the loose ball and, when Harvey Barnes was set free, he was not going to miss.

The turnaround was complete when defender Malick Thiaw forced over the goal-line from a corner which Arsenal had failed to defend - Dan Burn’s free header told you that someone, somewhere was not doing their job.

'We needed players with more energy and physicality,’ said Jaissle, explaining his half-time changes.

‘The tactics did not change, it was purely the front footed behaviour. Throw away the doubts, then you saw what is possible. We had Arsenal shaking. I hope we can carry on this feeling.’

Newcastle looked the most likely winners until Madueke burst inside two home jerseys and fired through Lukas Hornicek from 18 yards. Still, the hosts came back for more.

Arsenal had arrived intent on silencing St James’. In the end, they were grateful for the sound of the full-time whistle.

#1793. Liverpool injury update: Andoni Iraola makes worrying Ryan Gravenberch admission - "Not in a good place"

By Ben Knapton | 24 Nov 2026 17:13, Last updated: 24 Nov 2026 17:13

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola has dropped a worrying admission over Ryan Gravenberch's fitness ahead of Wednesday's Champions League clash with Club Brugge.

The Dutchman has missed each of the Reds' last three games with a heel fracture and was unsurprisingly not included in Liverpool's 22-man squad for the trip to the Jan Breydel Stadion.

Gravenberch had returned to training before Liverpool's 4-0 win over Manchester United in Sunday's Premier League affair, but the former Ajax man is still no closer to a competitive comeback.

After landing in Belgium, Iraola fielded questions from the media in his pre-game press conference, and he admitted that Gravenberch's injury was proving more complex to solve than initially anticipated.

"With Ryan, it's a bit more difficult," Iraola said. "He's having pain, the things in the fascia are difficult to solve. Sometimes he's managing the pain, but now he's not in a good place. Let's see if we can find ways to solve the problem but they are injuries that are not easy to solve normally."

While the exact nature and severity of Gravenberch's injury is not entirely clear, the Netherlands international may be suffering from Plantar fasciitis, which would fit Iraola's description.

An inflammation of the heel, Plantar fasciitis can take anywhere between four and 12 weeks to get better, and Gravenberch has already been out since the beginning of November.

As a result, the Dutchman may be missing until the end of January in the worst-case scenario, meaning he would firstly miss matches against Chelsea, Tottenham Hotspur, Porto and Aston Villa before the end of the year.

Liverpool then face Manchester United, Inter Milan and Everton again in the early weeks of 2027, and it remains to be seen if Gravenberch's complex issue has settled down by then.

The 24-year-old has set up one goal in 12 appearances for Liverpool so far this season, and in his absence, Alexis Mac Allister, Trey Nyoni, Dominik Szoboszlai and James McConnell will be competing for midfield minutes.

As well as delivering a negative update on Gravenberch, Iraola also revealed that Cody Gakpo would likely miss the weekend's Merseyside derby with Everton too.

The attacker hurt his calf while representing the Netherlands during the international break, although Iraola has insisted that his issue is not severe.

"With Cody, it's a soleus injury," Iraola added. "It's not big but we expect he'll be out for the weekend. But it's more predictable."

Giovanni Leoni (knee), Conor Bradley (knee) and Hugo Ekitike (Achilles) are also on the sidelines for Liverpool, who sit eighth in the Champions League league-phase table with nine points from their opening four fixtures.

James Penrice believes Rangers are acquiring the habit of winning ugly and grinding out results as their Premiership title challenge gathers momentum, but has warned they must address their tendency to surrender control after taking commanding positions in matches.

A gritty 3-2 victory over Aberdeen at Ibrox on Tuesday night brought Rangers to within a point of Celtic at the Premiership summit and extended their unbeaten sequence to 14 games. It was also another test of their resilience, with a disjointed first-half display giving way to an emphatic response after the interval, when Rangers struck three times in a blistering 12-minute spell.

The hosts had gone in at half-time trailing to Brad Lyons’ header, prompting McInnes to make a triple substitution and reshape his side. The changes had an immediate impact, with Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin all finding the net during a devastating spell early in the second half. However, Findlay Marshall’s reply ensured Rangers were unable to enjoy a comfortable conclusion to the match.

Penrice, who operated in a midfield three alongside Raskin and Dan Neil, praised the character shown by his team-mates to secure another welcome three points, but was equally candid about the frailties which threatened to undermine the victory.

“Very mixed, I think,” he said when asked for his assessment of an absorbing contest. “We conceded in the first half, but came flying out of the traps after the break. McInnes used the interval to make tactical changes, with Penrice crediting the substitutes for injecting the energy and intensity needed to wrestle control of the contest from Aberdeen.

“We made a couple of changes. I thought the boys that came on were brilliant, that real spark and energy,” he added. “We started the second half really well, but ultimately we need to score more. “Ultimately, it's not a bad trait to be scoring late on sometimes and winning games, but as players we want to make it as easy as possible. Again, we’ve made it hard but we’re still winning games and going on a wee bit of a run now, so hopefully that continues.”

Penrice’s versatility has become an increasingly valuable asset for McInnes. Primarily a left-back, he has also been deployed in central and wide positions as the manager continues to adapt his tactical approach to suit each fixture.

“I'm not bothered where, I’ll play absolutely anywhere to help the team,” he admitted. “It’s a massive thing for me. It's not alien to us, we've done it numerous times this season, guys playing in different positions.

“I've played in the middle, I've played out wide, so we should all be used to it now and we are. It just takes that adjustment period on the pitch but us as players we've got a responsibility when there's a plan in place and something's not going right we fix it ourselves. We don't need to go to the side and I think that's what the gaffer is looking for. He's looking for us to take responsibility on the pitch and we've got that now.”

Rangers have little time to dwell on their latest victory, with Falkirk due at Ibrox next on Saturday, a fixture that offers McInnes’ side the chance to leapfrog Celtic and move top of the Premiership table, having closed the gap on the leaders with their comeback win over Aberdeen.

“It's a massive incentive, but the league's not won in November,” Penrice declared. “It will be a difficult game. Falkirk are playing well and they've travelled well away from home. So we'll need to be on it. We can't go into the game on Saturday like we were tonight. We need to be better. We just need to concentrate on ourselves, it's another game to tick off, one at a time.”

Baur was recently ruled out for up to 10 weeks with ankle ligament damage but manager Martin O’Neill had been waiting to see how the German international reacted once his protective boot was off.

Baur could miss the rest of the league stage though and O’Neill has acted before setting off for Portugal.

With Benjamin Nygren nursing a heel problem, O’Neill started with a midfield three of Callum McGregor, Luke McCowan and Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain on Saturday, while Oliver Sorensen is another option.

Meanwhile, O’Neill has challenged Celtic to complete their Europa League comeback after resurrecting hopes against Besiktas.

Celtic were heading for a fourth straight defeat and bottom spot when they went behind against the Turks but they were inspired by the introduction of Camilo Duran, Callum Osmand and Colby Donovan and sealed a 3-2 win.

They now face away games against Torreense and Omonia Nicosia as they bid to move up the table.

Looking back at their recent win, O’Neill told Celtic Player: “I thought it was terrific. Really terrific.

“Besiktas are a very fine football team. Very fine side. They were expecting to win and win handsomely. They’ve spent a lot of money. I think their wage bill is in excess of £100million. So from that aspect, it was a terrific win.

“The character of the side was really brilliant. Really, really brilliant to win so late, and to win in the fashion in which we did was terrific. So it gives us a little bit of a chance and we have to go and try to do something for these next two away games.

“If we make it through to the qualifying stages, it will be the first time any team has been beaten in their first three games and made it.

“So that in itself should be a target for us. The games are not easy, we know that. We need to win at least one of these two away games and we might even need four points to give us a chance in the last two matches.

“We have to take confidence from recent games and take that into the game on Thursday.”

Torreense sit 13th in the Portuguese second tier and will host Celtic 60 miles away from their home in Leiria, as their own stadium only has about 2,500 seats.

But they have already beaten Lillestrom and Ararat-Armenia in the Europa League and took the lead against Sunderland before the Premier League side netted a stoppage-time winner.

“They won the Portuguese Cup against Sporting Lisbon, which is some achievement,” O’Neill said. “I’ve been learning as much as I can about them and watching footage.”

Asked about his side’s prospects of making it through, head coach Vrancken, whose side won 8-0 at Dundee on Saturday, said: “Confident. You have to always push it until it’s over.

“So it’s all good things and we have to keep pushing. When the bodies are coming back, it’s also good for the mental side of it. For the other players who are already playing a lot of games, it’s also a good thing and it’s also good motivation.”

Vrancken hopes Landry Kabore’s double at Dundee can help the striker get back on track after what he viewed as a loss of confidence since he was substituted following a poor display in the 2-2 draw at home to Rapid Vienna in August.

“He had a difficult period,” said Vrancken. “I remember here at the home game when we brought him in and he lost every ball he had.

“But I’m just happy for him that he could cope with the situation and that he could manage to show himself in training sessions. He can be also an example for others who are in the same situation.”

#1785. KILMARNOCK 2 ABERDEEN 4: Dazzling Dons get a Frick pick-up but it's more misery for McCann's men

Published: 15:33 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 16:15 EST, 21 November 2026

Having been bored senseless by the football offered up under Stephen Robinson, Aberdeen supporters were – at the very least – crying out for the next appointment to provide some sort of entertainment to get excited about over the dark winter months.

In Mario Frick, they may have got their man. Whether or not the former Luzern boss will be a success at Pittodrie is anyone’s guess. But on this evidence, it’s going to be a lot of fun watching him have a go.

At times, they were scintillating here on their way to a thrilling win which moved them five clear of their hosts and provided some much-needed breathing room ahead of a tricky upcoming schedule which involves trips to Ibrox and Tynecastle, as well as two home clashes against the Dundee clubs.

Yes, it wasn’t perfect. Far from it, in fact. Defensively, they were far too open. Kilmarnock just weren’t good enough to take full advantage.

But you suspect that will be forgiven to an extent as long as they can play with this level of panache and aggression going forward.

Findlay Marshall celebrates after scoring the Dons' fourth goal at Rugby Park

Frick has arrived with the promise of bringing ‘heavy metal’ football to Pittodrie. It’s taken a little over 90 minutes to understand what he's talking about.

‘It was very chaotic,’ he admitted. ‘It's quite different to Switzerland, because there is technicality, but it’s not as physical as it was today.

‘It was difficult. We were lucky as well because Killie, especially in the second half, played very well, but I think at the end it's a deserved victory.

‘When the players were young, they didn’t think about mistakes, didn’t think about any negatives.

‘They played only to win for fun, and I told them to play as if they were young players and I think, especially first half, it was very good.

‘You don't know what's going on or what can happen in this first game, so I'm very happy we won.’

Frick shows his delight after tasting victory in his first match in charge of Aberdeen

Kilmarnock spurned a golden opportunity to take a sixth-minute lead at the end of a rapid counter-attack, with Joe Hugill finding himself all alone in the Dons box.

The striker took a heavy first touch, allowing Marius Muller to quickly narrow the angle and block the effort. It’s easy to see why Hugill has found the back of the net just twice this year.

And the hosts were made to pay for that miss within 90 seconds as Aberdeen went in front.

For the umpteenth time this season, Killie failed to clear their lines under little pressure, with Stuart Armstrong teeing up Kevin Nisbet to sweep home a lovely finish from the edge of the area. The unsighted Nico Mantl in the Killie goal didn’t even move.

Mind you, he should have done significantly better four minutes later as Nisbet notched his second of the afternoon.

The keeper’s positioning as the Dons striker stepped up to send a low free-kick in off the post was as poor as it gets.

You got the feeling that the walls would have caved in had Aberdeen grabbed a third, but a brief drop-off in intensity from Frick’s side enabled Killie to drag themselves back into the contest.

A bit of pinball outside the Dons box saw the ball fall favourably for skipper Greg Kiltie 12 yards out, who adjusted his body brilliantly to drill beyond Muller on the half-volley.

Yet with a defence as dodgy as this, manager Neil McCann can never feel overly confident.

Ante Palaversa – terrific on his first appearance of the season – was given far too much time in the centre circle to get his head up and pick out Nesta Guinness-Walker on the left.

He glided past MJ Kamson-Kamara as if he wasn’t there before dinking a ball right on to the head of Brad Lyons, who rose completely unopposed to power home against his former employers.

If Killie continue to defend like this, relegation is a certainty. Will the manager even get the chance to turn it around? Going off the abuse being hurled in his direction from the home punters, his jacket is evidently on a shoogly peg. Many fans have already made up their mind.

Nisbet's free-kick finds the net for his second as the Dons take control of the game

Michael Schjonning-Larsen’s deflected effort from 20 yards shortly after the restart looked destined for the goal before Muller instinctively leapt to his right to claw it away on the line. It was a superb stop.

Goodness knows what the keeper was thinking as he tried to pass out from the six-yard line, playing it straight to the feet of Tyreece John-Jules – only just on the park – who steadied himself before finishing.

You would have stuck your house on Nisbet putting this one to bed with five minutes remaining, however with just Mantl to beat, he pulled his left-footed effort wide.

Findlay Marshall showed him how it’s done with stoppage-time looming, running half the length of the field before drilling low into the corner to consign Killie to another sobering defeat.

McCann said: ‘I probably sound like a broken record, but we create really big, big chances, and we don't take them.

‘We're letting games pass us by. We're giving teams the opportunity to start ahead of us because of the goals we're conceding and then it's difficult to work back.’

#1784. GdS: ‘Turbo Milan’ – how Frosinone were dismantled by five-star counter-attacking display

AC Milan put in one of their best performances under Ruben Amorim so far to sweep aside Frosinone at San Siro.

La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below) begin a report by writing that Lazio, Roma and Juventus also had fun this weekend, scoring a flurry of goals in their victories, but it is Milan that might just come away from the round 12 feeling best.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Within 20 minutes, the Rossoneri had already blown the game wide open, eventually putting five past their opponents. All of them were spectacular, lightning-fast, and following the same pattern: every single one a counter-attack.

It was a throwback style of football, yet infused with the visionary approach of Amorim, making it both fresh and truly beautiful to watch. There may not be official statistics on this, but conceding from five lethal transitions feels like a record as Frosinone’s strategy certainly went beyond mere self-sabotage.

Yet, on days like this, this Milan – an enigma to its opponents, with fluid movement and interchangeable positioning – are a truly daunting prospect. When Adrien Rabiot, Diego Moreira, Luka Modrić and others perform at such a high level, we see the potential of this side.

The Diavolo have secured five wins in their last six league matches, yet in Europe, they have suffered three defeats in four games. Will Thursday’s clash against Olympiacos help restore the balance?

There was nothing balanced about the game between Milan and Frosinone. It is true that Alvini’s incredibly bold (perhaps even reckless) side tried to go toe-to-toe with their opponents for an hour by attacking, playing long balls, and taking on defenders.

Yet, beyond this emphasis on a specific style of play, one could make more concrete assessments. The coach clearly understood how vital Raimondo is to a team featuring such direct and creative wingers, Ghedjemis on the right and Kvernadze (who was rather ineffective yesterday) on the left.

Raimondo was the perfect focal point for them and without him, things had already gone poorly against Cagliari. Alvini attempted to make adjustments but got it wrong: he abandoned his 4-2-3-1 formation in favour of a back three (Calvani, Monterisi, Cittadini).

All this was undermined by a senseless tendency to push too high, maintaining a defensive line 57 metres from their own goal within a 3-4-3 setup that lacked a true striker, opting instead for a ‘false’ one in Schmid. Every time they lost possession, it resulted in a counter-attack and often a goal.

It might seem odd to start with Frosinone rather than the brilliance of Milan, but there’s no denying that the visitors played their part in the spectacle. This is a match that future opponents will need to study in minute detail, because Milan on the counter are a goal-scoring machine.

Amorim, too, has a knack for springing surprises, though as always the guessing game regarding his actual tactical setup for the day begins the moment the whistle blows. For example, it was not a back four as it appeared on paper.

Instead, the system actually gradually morphed into a 3-5-2, with Rabiot operating as a highly advanced right-sided central midfielder, almost an attacking midfielder. The key lies in the connection between the Frenchman and the stratospheric Moreira, who surged down the centre often.

Keeping everything running at full throttle was the incredible playmaking of Modrić, who also serves as the team’s primary ball-winner. So much for being a ‘pensioner’.

Milan proved flawless in exploiting both structural weaknesses and individual errors. Frosinone’s DNA is defined by a headlong, aggressive approach, but the opening goal – stemming from a sequence on the right flank involving Modrić and Rabiot – ended up as an own goal by Calvani.

Just four minutes in, and the match was effectively decided. While Frosinone usually thrive on quick, darting attacks, here the roles were reversed. Another full-pitch surge, initiated by Ramos winning the ball from Calvani and carried forward by Moreira and Rabiot, left the Portuguese player unmarked to make it 2-0.

Only a reckless back pass from Musah gifted Masini a goal to pull it back to 2-1. In the second half, however, Amorim addressed the one area that looked shaky: he withdrew Bartesaghi – who had been struggling against Ghedjemis – shifting Musah to full-back and pairing Jashari with Modrić.

It paid off immediately: Jashari broke away and fired home the 3-1 following yet another rapid transition. And that wasn’t the only one: Pulisic surged clear on his own after a Frosinone corner (4-1), and Cissé, having just come on, joined the fray at full throttle to add the fifth (5-1).

There were many top performances. Rabiot is like a freight train and deserved a goal. He had to settle for three assists (bringing his total to seven). Moreira is versatile, playing as a wing-back, a central midfielder, or a winger, much like he did for Belgium when they caused Italy so much trouble.

Ramos also moved well outside of his goal. Cissé was an absolute handful: he came on and scorrd, playing as a striker after the Portuguese felt a tweak. He did so with an effortless grace that makes him impossible for his markers to handle.

The end result is that Milan are back in fourth. The competition is fierce, but the Rossoneri are right there in the mix, and eventually, some of the others will stumble. Take Inter, for example. Frosinone need to rethink their strategy while waiting for the return of Raimondo.

They’ve overachieved so far, but now they might need to be a bit more prudent. And what about Milan? If they don’t turn their trip to Athens into a Greek tragedy, perhaps their European campaign can get back on track, too.
